newsitem.title: USA: Reuters Asset Allocation Poll (New York) July 1.
newsitem.headline: Reuters Asset Allocation Poll (New York) July 1.

text.p: U.S.-based global equity fund managers made subtle shifts in their portfolio weightings over the past two months, culling funds out of the U.S. and moving them into other parts of the globe.

Despite the 19-percent swell in the Dow Jones Industrial Average since the turn of the year, some fund managers fled the great American wave for calmer seas in emerging markets and continental and Eastern Europe.

A Reuters global asset allocation poll of global bond and equity portfolios showed the average U.S. weighting of global equity funds slipped to 32 percent by the end of June from just over 34 percent in late April.
When measured against the Morgan Stanley Capital International Index, a widely accepted global benchmark, many of the respondents were still underweight U.S. equities.

The weighting of shares in the Latin America sector increased to 7.2 percent from almost 3.0 percent during the same survey period. The other European sector grew to almost 16 percent in June from 12 percent in the previous survey.

The continuance of swift corporate restructurings in continental Europe is improving shareholder value there, said USAA co-portfolio manager Al Sebastian, who manages about $1.4 billion in international equities.

"There is more opportunity in continental Europe to find restructuring candidates because the U.S. has done most of its restructuring, and we just feel that Europe is still significantly behind the U.S. in terms of running its businesses more efficiently," he said.
Eastern Europe has benefitted from investments from neighboring Western Europe, Sebastian said.
"There is a lot of production being shifted out of high-cost areas of Western Europe into Eastern Europe," he added.
In emerging markets, some Latin American countries have made significant reductions in their inflation rates and stabilized prices, helping to fuel economic growth.

Lisa Cullen, investment strategist at Merrill, Lynch and Co Inc, said Mexico has showed significant improvement over the last six months, given the country's success in repaying its obligations from its 1994 financial crisis.
"(Mexico's) emerging debt markets are roaring right now, and we think that money from their debt markets will move to their equity markets," she said.
Other investors continued to seek value in Japanese equities, evidenced by the steady 14 percent average weighting in June versus April.
Among bond markets, the U.S. figured more prominently as allocation depended largely on a slowing economy in the second half of the year.
On average, the U.S. debt allocations edged up to 37.5 percent of assets from 35.5 percent.
David Bricker, vice president of private banking and investment services at Bank of America, said his position in U.S. debt was relatively neutral in terms of a balanced type account.
"Clearly, the economy is slowing and the (Federal Reserve) will take a wait-and-see attitude," Bricker said, referring to the central bank's position on interest rates.
Country recommendations for the June survey were collected in late June. Full results of the survey follow. Monthly polls are also done from London (key GB/ASSET F9) and Tokyo (key JP/ASSET F9.)
